analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal standard workweek from 40 hours to 32 with required overtime.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Fair Labor Standards Act to define overtime as any work beyond 32 hours in a week, phased in over three years (38, then 36, then 34, then 32 hours). It also would have required overtime pay for workdays over 8 hours and double-time pay for workdays over 12 hours. The bill was introduced on March 1, 2023, referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, and received no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act would gain a shorter standard workweek: hours worked beyond 32 a week, 8 a day, or 12 a day would trigger overtime premiums, making employers either pay more or schedule fewer hours. Workers who keep the same schedule and pay would, in effect, get a four-day week. Note that salaried workers exempt from the law's overtime rules would not benefit directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers covered by overtime law

how_it_helps.text: ReDefines the standard workweek as 32 hours, phased in over three years (38 hours the first year, 36 the second, 34 the third, 32 after that), so hours beyond that must be paid at time-and-a-half.
Adds daily overtime protections: time-and-a-half after 8 hours in a workday and double-time after 12 hours, giving workers leverage over long shifts rather than only weekly totals.

Employers facing overtime costs could respond by hiring more workers to split hours, which the bill's structure encourages by making each additional hour of any employee expensive beyond the new thresholds.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who rely on long weekly schedules — particularly in industries like trucking, retail, restaurants, and manufacturing — would bear higher payroll costs unless they cap hours at 32 or add staff. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through prices, and some workers who prefer more than 32 hours a week could see their hours or take-home pay capped by scheduling changes.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not mandate that weekly pay stay the same at fewer hours; employers could reduce hours to avoid overtime, leaving workers earning less unless they land additional hours elsewhere.
Salaries workers exempt from the FLSA's overtime rules would see no change, so the benefit is limited to hourly, non-exempt employees.
A 32-hour standard would raise labor costs sharply for industries structured around long hours, an objection that businesses and the bill's opponents could be expected to raise in committee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For hourly workers, the bill would create a real potential gain: fewer hours for the same standard, or premium pay for every hour beyond 32. The main honest costs are that employers could cut hours instead of paying premiums, leaving some workers with smaller paychecks, and that industries built on long shifts would face genuine cost increases. Because it died without any committee review or cost estimates, there was no official assessment of how large those effects would be.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act on March 1, 2023, with Reps. Jayapal and Schakowsky as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
That referral was the last action in its history; the committee took no further steps, and the bill never reached the House floor.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced higher payroll costs under a 32-hour standard are better off, because the bill never advanced. Workers who wanted a shorter federally guaranteed workweek gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid the new overtime

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors; the referral to committee was the last recorded action on it.

for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all from the Democratic Party.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without a hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the 118th Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Chamber majority controlling the committee and floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Controlled which bills received committee time and floor votes; no bill reducing the standard workweek was brought forward in this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and a Republican-controlled House committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Employers of long-hour hourly workforces (retail, restaurants, logistics, trucking)
industries.note: Overtime would kick in past 32 hours a week and past 8 hours a day, raising the cost of every long schedule. These industries' interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the shorter hours and premium pay workers would have gained.

Workers covered by the FLSA would gain premium pay for hours beyond 32 a week and 8 a day, or shorter standard schedules. Unions had long sought a shorter workweek, and a bill like this strengthens their bargaining position by making long hours costlier.
